title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 351
paragraphs: After Mykerinos, the priests said, Asychis became king of Egypt, and he built for Hephaistos the temple gateway that faces the sunrise — by far the most beautiful and largest of the gateways. While all of them have figures carved upon them and countless other architectural ornaments, this one has them far more than the rest. In this king's reign, they told me, as the circulation of money was very slow, a law was passed for the Egyptians allowing a man to borrow the money he needed by offering as security the dead body of his father. An additional clause was added: the lender was to have a claim on the whole burial chamber belonging to the borrower, and the borrower who offered this security, if he refused to repay the debt, would be subject to this penalty — that neither he himself would be allowed burial when he died, either in the family tomb or any other, nor would he be allowed to bury any kinsman who died. Wishing to surpass the kings of Egypt before him, this king left as his memorial a pyramid that he made of bricks, on which there is an inscription carved in stone that says: “Do not despise me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, for I surpass them as much as Zeus surpasses the other gods. For with a pole they struck into the lake, and whatever mud stuck to the pole, they gathered up and made into bricks, and in this way they finished me.”
Such were the deeds this king performed;
